prompt: Assume a 17,000 km fibre path at 200,000 km/s. What propagation floor does that imply for RTT and for four sequential round trips over this same path?

options.text: About 57 ms, so a well-tuned server could serve Sydney from London quickly
options.explanation: 57 ms is the one-way time for light in a *vacuum* (17,000 / 300,000 s). Fibre is slower, and a round trip goes there and back.

options.text: About 85 ms, so three round trips fit in a quarter of a second
options.explanation: 85 ms is the one-way time in fibre. A round trip doubles it.

options.text: About 340 ms, because each round trip crosses the distance four times
options.explanation: A round trip crosses the distance twice (there and back), not four times.

options.text: About 170 ms for the assumed fibre path, so four sequential trips over it require at least 680 ms before other delays
options.explanation: Correct. One-way: 17,000 / 200,000 = 85 ms; round trip ≈ 170 ms. Cables don't follow the great circle, so real RTTs are higher still. Only moving servers or edges closer beats this.

workedExample:
Divide distance by speed, then double for the return trip:

```formula
t_one = d / v
t_one = 17,000 km / 200,000 km/s
t_one = 0.085 s = 85 ms
RTT_min = 2 × t_one = 170 ms
T_4 = 4 × RTT_min = 680 ms
where
t_one: the one-way propagation time, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
d: the length of the fibre path, 17,000 kilometres (km)
v: the speed of light in fibre, about 200,000 kilometres per second (km/s)
RTT_min: the propagation floor for one round trip
T_4: the minimum time for four sequential round trips
km: kilometre
km/s: kilometres per second
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
In words: 85 ms each way, 170 ms per round trip, and 680 ms for four, before any queueing or longer cable routes.
```

Four sequential trips over that same path take at least 680 ms. This does not automatically describe a cold HTTPS request: DNS may use a nearby resolver, while a normal TCP/TLS1.3 request needs three origin round trips. Protocol changes reduce trip counts; endpoint placement, physical route and transmission medium affect propagation time.

link.title: High Performance Browser Networking: Primer on latency

prompt: A network operator can inspect your decrypted IP packets on café Wi-Fi. You access `https://shop.example.com/cart` using plain UDP DNS, no VPN/proxy and no ECH. What can this passive observer learn directly? Select all that apply.

options.text: The IP address of the server you connect to
options.explanation: Correct. IP headers must be readable for packets to be routed, so the destination address is always visible.

options.text: The path `/cart` and your session cookie
options.explanation: These are inside the encrypted HTTP request. TLS hides the method, path, headers, cookies and body.

options.text: The hostname `shop.example.com`, from the DNS query
options.explanation: Correct. Classic DNS over UDP port 53 is unencrypted, so the query and answer are visible. DoH or DoT would hide this hop.

options.text: The hostname `shop.example.com`, from the TLS ClientHello
options.explanation: Correct. Without ECH, the SNI extension carries the hostname in the clear so the server can choose a certificate.

options.text: The exact prices on the page
options.explanation: The response body is encrypted. An observer sees only its approximate size and timing.

workedExample:
1. In this scenario the observer sees destination IP headers; a VPN would instead expose its outer endpoint.
2. Plain UDP DNS reveals the queried hostname.
3. Without ECH, SNI reveals the hostname again.
4. TLS encrypts the HTTP path, cookies and body. Timing, size and destination IP can still leak information; encrypted DNS plus ECH does not guarantee site anonymity.
